You are on a roof or in a crawl space when the next estimate request calls. An AI voice agent answers, learns what the job is, and puts the site visit on your calendar.

The phone rings while your hands are full

For most small contractors, AI for contractors starts with one job: an AI receptionist that answers estimate requests while you are working, so the call becomes a booked site visit instead of a voicemail you return at dark.

Homeowners shopping for a project rarely call just one company. The Federal Trade Commission's advice on avoiding home improvement scams tells homeowners to get written estimates from several firms. That is good advice for them, and it means a caller who reaches your voicemail can simply dial the next contractor on the list.

We set up an AI voice agent on HighLevel that picks up those calls, asks the questions you ask on a first call, and puts the estimate visit on your calendar. You still do the selling, the measuring and the pricing. The agent just makes sure the conversation starts.

What a good estimate call captures

You decide which of these the agent asks and in what order. The answers arrive by email and in your CRM, so you can decide from the truck whether the drive is worth it.

  • The jobRoof repair or replacement, kitchen or bath remodel, addition, deck, panel upgrade, new circuit, whatever your trade covers, and whether it is residential or commercial.
  • The scope, roughlyHow many rooms, how many squares, how old the roof is, whether the house has had work done before. Rough answers are fine; you will measure it yourself.
  • TimelineIs this urgent, this season, or next year? Is there an insurance claim, a closing date or an inspection driving it?
  • Budget range, if you want itSome contractors want the question asked, others find it puts callers off. The agent follows your choice.
  • Address and accessWhere the job is, who will be there, gate codes, and whether the caller owns the property.
  • PhotosThe agent can ask the caller to email photos of the area, so you see it before you drive out.
  • How they found youUseful for knowing which ads, referrals or signs are working.

Why the agent never prices a job sight unseen

A number given over the phone before anyone has looked at the job becomes the number the customer remembers. If the decking is rotten, the wiring is aluminum or the wall you planned to move is load bearing, the real price will be different, and you start the relationship explaining why.

The same FTC guidance tells homeowners to compare written estimates and ask why prices differ, which is the conversation you want to have in person, after you have seen the work. So the agent books the visit and, when a caller pushes for a price, gives the answer you wrote: that the price comes after the estimate visit, or a published starting price if you choose to share one.

That is also why AI for general contractors works best as a front desk, not an estimator. It organizes the request; you price it.

Roofers, remodelers, electricians and general contractors

The calls differ by trade, so the setup does too. These are starting points we adjust with you.

TradeWhat callers usually askWhat the agent collectsWhere it stops
RoofersLeak repairs, storm damage, full replacement, whether you work with insurance claimsRoof age, leak location, whether there is an open claim, address for the inspectionNo opinion on whether insurance will pay, no price before the inspection
RemodelersKitchens, baths, basements, additions, how far out you are bookingRooms involved, what they want changed, timeline, budget range if you ask for itNo design advice, no estimate until you have walked the space
ElectriciansOutages, panel upgrades, EV chargers, new circuits, whether you do commercial workIs power out, is anything sparking or hot, what the job is, addressNo electrical instructions; a downed line gets your approved safety line to stay away and call 911
General contractorsWhole projects, permits, who handles the subs, whether you take small jobsProject type, plans or drawings on hand, timeline, decision makersNo commitment on schedule or subcontractors; that is your call after the meeting

An AI receptionist for electricians needs the clearest safety rules of the four. The Electrical Safety Foundation's guidance on downed power lines is to stay away and call 911, so that is the kind of line we load, and the agent reads it word for word instead of improvising. AI for electrical contractors otherwise looks a lot like it does for any trade: answer, qualify, book, follow up.

Storm season for roofers: when every phone in town rings at once

After hail or high wind, roofing calls arrive in a wave. The FTC's advice on avoiding scams after weather emergencies tells homeowners to ask for IDs, licenses and proof of insurance before paying anyone, and its home repair scam advice lists a contractor who knocks on the door because they are "in the area" as a warning sign. A roofing company that answers its phone, takes the details calmly and books inspections in order is the opposite of what homeowners are being warned about.

Roofing is seasonal in other ways too. The Bureau of Labor Statistics notes that in northern states roofing work may be limited during the winter months, and that roofers may work overtime during the busy summer months. On those long days, the phone is the first thing to fall behind.

  1. Calls picked up while you are on the roof. The agent answers when the office line would otherwise ring out, and every caller is asked the same storm questions.
  2. Inspections booked into the slots you open. You decide how many a day; the agent fills them and takes a waiting list when they run out.
  3. Honest expectations. The agent tells callers what you want said about your schedule, without promising a date you cannot keep.
  4. No pressure. It does not push anyone to sign or to file a claim. It collects details and books.

Lead follow-up in the CRM after the estimate

The call is only the start. Many contractor jobs are lost after the estimate, when the homeowner goes quiet and nobody follows up. Every caller becomes a contact in a HighLevel pipeline with stages that match how you work: new request, visit booked, estimate sent, won, lost.

  • An automated email follow-up goes out if an estimate has had no answer after the number of days you choose
  • The call summary is saved on the contact, so before the visit you can reread what the homeowner described
  • Finished jobs can trigger a review request by email
  • With AI Pro, an outbound voice agent can call back old estimates at the start of a new season

Texting is not live yet. Voice works today. Text messages (missed call text back, text reminders and texted review requests) switch on once carrier approval clears; that approval is the A2P 10DLC registration US carriers require for business texting from a regular local number. Until then, follow-ups, reminders and review requests go out by email.

Who this fits, and who it does not

A good fit if

  • You run a small construction business and you are the one who answers the phone
  • Estimate requests come in while you are on a job and you return them at night
  • You want callers qualified before you drive out
  • You already know what you want asked on a first call

Not a fit for, and what it does not do

  • Price a job sight unseen or give a bid over the phone
  • Dispatch crews, schedule subcontractors or replace the person who runs your jobs
  • Give repair, electrical or safety instructions you have not written and approved
  • Advise on insurance claims, permits or code questions
  • Connect to your estimating or project software until we have confirmed, for your account, that it can

Questions contractors ask about AI

How can AI help in construction?

For a small construction business, the most practical help is in the office work around the job: answering calls while you are on site, collecting the details of each estimate request, scheduling site visits, and following up on estimates you sent. That is the part we set up. AI does not replace estimating, bidding, inspections or safety on the jobsite, and we do not sell it as if it did.

What is the best AI for contractors?

The one that does a specific job you need done, and that you have tested yourself. For most small contractors that job is answering estimate calls and following up, not a general chatbot. Before you pay anyone, call their line and pretend to be a homeowner asking for a roof or remodel estimate. Ours is answered by an AI receptionist, so you can do exactly that. The guide to choosing an AI agency lists more questions to ask.

Can an AI receptionist for contractors give estimates?

No, and it should not. A price for a roof, a kitchen or a panel upgrade depends on what you find on site. The agent collects the scope, timeline, address and, if you want it to ask, a budget range, then books an estimate visit. If a caller presses for a number, it says the price comes after you see the job, or states a starting price only if you have chosen to publish one.

Does AI for electrical contractors handle emergency calls?

It answers them and routes them by your rules. An electrical contractor might want a power outage at a business or sparking at a panel transferred to the on-call electrician, and a request for new outlets booked for later. A caller who reports a downed power line hears the safety line you approved, such as stay away from it and call 911, and you get an alert. The agent never gives electrical instructions.
